title: Review an API endpoint that trusts an object ID from the client
description: Problem: Review an API endpoint that trusts an object ID from the client. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: An API endpoint accepts an identifier directly from the request body or route and uses it to query or update data without verifying that the authenticated user owns that resource. An attacker who knows or guesses another user's identifier can read or modify data that does not belong to them. This is an Insecure Direct Object Reference, or IDOR, and it is one of the most common and most impactful API vulnerabilities.

items: Understand how object identifiers flow from client to database in a typical REST API
Learn why client-supplied IDs must be validated against the current user's ownership or permissions
Identify the difference between horizontal privilege escalation (accessing another user's data) and vertical escalation (gaining admin rights)
Apply defense-in-depth: ownership checks, resource-based authorization, and opaque identifiers

terms.definition: Insecure Direct Object Reference: accessing a resource by its identifier without verifying that the caller is authorized to access it.
Accessing data or actions belonging to another user with the same privilege level.
Accessing data or actions belonging to a higher privilege level, such as an admin function from a regular user account.
Checking whether the current user owns or is permitted to access the specific resource identified by the request, rather than relying solely on route or role checks.

data.text: IDOR vulnerabilities appear in every type of application: SaaS dashboards, mobile APIs, and internal admin tools. Automated scanners detect them easily, and real-world exploitation is straightforward: change the ID in the URL from 123 to 124 and observe the response. A single missing ownership check can expose thousands of user records, and the breach may go unnoticed for months because the API returns 200 OK rather than an error.

data.title: IDOR is a data breach waiting to happen
data.text: If an endpoint returns data based solely on an ID from the client, assume an attacker will enumerate it. Ownership checks are not optional; they are the baseline for any endpoint that touches user data.

The vulnerable endpoint receives an order ID from the route, queries the database, and returns the result. There is no check that the order belongs to the authenticated user. An attacker who knows a valid order ID for another user can retrieve that order's contents, shipping address, and payment details.

data.title: Vulnerable endpoint
data.content: An endpoint that trusts the client-supplied ID without ownership verification:

data.text: The fix is to scope every query by the current user's identity. The user ID comes from the authenticated context, not the request body. Additionally, use non-sequential identifiers such as GUIDs or ULIDs to make enumeration harder, though ownership checks are still required even with opaque IDs.

data.title: Secure endpoint with ownership check
data.content: Filter by the current user's ID before returning data:

cards.title: Ownership filter in query
cards.description: Add the current user's ID to every WHERE clause.
cons: Easy to forget in a new endpoint
Does not protect against leaked admin tokens

cards.title: Opaque identifiers
cards.description: Use random GUIDs or ULIDs instead of sequential integers.
pros: No information leakage about record count

cards.title: Resource-based authorization policies
cards.description: Use a centralized policy or requirement that checks ownership before the action executes.

cards.title: Per-record encryption
cards.description: Encrypt sensitive fields so that even if the record is accessed, the data is unreadable.

data.title: Secure API design rules
items: Every endpoint that returns or modifies data must filter by the current user's ID
Never trust route parameters, query strings, or request bodies as the sole source of authorization
Use resource-based authorization for any endpoint that accesses records by ID
Return 404 instead of 403 when a resource is not found or not owned; this prevents enumeration
Log access to sensitive records with user ID and resource ID for audit trails

data.title: Return 404, not 403
data.text: Returning 404 when a user does not own a resource prevents attackers from enumerating valid IDs. If you return 403, the attacker knows the ID exists and can try another one.

items.question: Are sequential IDs really a vulnerability?
items.answer: By themselves, no. But they make enumeration trivial. Combine sequential IDs with missing ownership checks and you have a data breach. Use opaque IDs as a second layer of defense.

items.question: Does GraphQL have the same problem?
items.answer: Yes. GraphQL queries can request any field by ID. Ownership checks must be applied at the resolver level, not just at the transport or schema level.

items.question: How do I test for IDOR?
items.answer: Create two users, log in as user A, and try to access a resource owned by user B. The API should return 404. Automate this in your integration test suite.

items.question: What about batch endpoints?
items.answer: Batch endpoints amplify IDOR because a single request can access many records. Filter each item in the batch by the current user's ID, and reject the entire batch if any item fails the check.

data.title: Audit an API for IDOR
data.description: Review a set of API endpoints and identify every route that accepts a client-supplied ID without verifying ownership.
steps: List all GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE endpoints that accept an ID parameter
For each endpoint, trace the query to verify it filters by the current user
Write an integration test that creates two users, accesses user A's resource as user B, and expects 404
Add resource-based authorization policies to any endpoint that fails the test
Document the fix in the pull request description
data.expectedOutcome: Every endpoint that accesses data by ID includes an ownership filter. The integration test suite catches any new IDOR regression.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Client-supplied IDs are untrusted input, not authorization
Always filter queries by the authenticated user's identity
Automate IDOR checks in your integration test suite
data.takeaway: If an API trusts the client for authorization, the client becomes the attacker.
